title: Industry views on Treasury climate and nature economics: costs, certainty and competitiveness
label: 4 November 2026 · HM Treasury and the economics of climate and nature
summary: Representatives from the motor, ceramics and energy industries told the Environmental Audit Committee that Treasury tax and fiscal policy is inconsistent and often undermines investment in decarbonisation. They praised some supply-side support, warned that high electricity and gas costs damage competitiveness, challenged the timing and design of electric-vehicle taxation, and urged recycling of carbon revenues and clearer long-term signals to enable industrial transition.

chapters.title: Overall view: policies are mixed and timing matters
chapters.takeaway: All three industries welcome some support but say tax and fiscal policy is inconsistent, sends mixed signals, and often raises costs that harm competitiveness.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We are looking at whether Treasury tax and fiscal policies give industries clear incentives to invest in lower-carbon practices. Gentlemen, your quick verdict?

turns.speaker: Matthew Croucher
turns.text: Short answer: no. There are helpful measures—DRIVE35 support for EVs, for example—but overall the UK is an expensive place to do business, particularly because energy costs are high.

turns.speaker: Andrew McDermott
turns.text: From ceramics' view it is similar: the framework isn't coherent. Policies add cost to meet environmental aims but often weaken competitiveness and can push production abroad rather than cut global emissions.

turns.speaker: Adam Berman
turns.text: Treasury understands the opportunity of the energy transition and has backed supply-side schemes, but the demand side—getting homes and businesses to electrify—isn't consistently supported in fiscal policy.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: So the common theme is inconsistent signals and high energy costs limiting investment in decarbonisation?

turns.speaker: Matthew Croucher
turns.text: Yes—especially timing. The eVED announcement in 2028 came when the industry and consumers need encouragement, not a new tax signal.

chapters.title: Motors, EVs and taxation: mixed messages and practical barriers
chapters.takeaway: Manufacturers back electrification but warn that planning, taxes, charging costs and residual values still make the transition costly and uncertain.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Matthew, the SMMT represents the whole motor industry. Do Treasury policies support your members to move to EVs while keeping the industry competitive?

turns.speaker: Matthew Croucher
turns.text: Not coherently. Support has been stop-start: zero-rated VED and the plug-in grant were removed and then partly reinstated. eVED due in 2028 looks like an EV tax at the wrong time.

turns.speaker: Jonathan Davies
turns.text: Should the UK have pushed more for hydrogen like Japan, rather than following the global move to battery electrics?

turns.speaker: Matthew Croucher
turns.text: Industry is split but the global trend is towards electrification. Hydrogen has niche uses; infrastructure is almost non-existent here for hydrogen vehicles.

turns.speaker: Jonathan Davies
turns.text: If the ZEV mandate slowed, what would that mean?

turns.speaker: Matthew Croucher
turns.text: Manufacturers would welcome a gentler trajectory. There are many new BEV models, but consumers still need incentives and public charging is often costly compared with home charging.

turns.speaker: Matthew Croucher
turns.text: We also need clarity on eVED implementation—things like eVED Connect and how vehicle connectivity data will be used raise privacy and practical questions.

chapters.title: Energy costs and electrification: demand-side support is missing
chapters.takeaway: Energy UK says supply-side policy (like Contracts for Difference) has worked, but high electricity prices and weak demand-side incentives are blocking wider electrification.

turns.speaker: Adam Berman
turns.text: Supply-side support has delivered large-scale renewables, but the big gap is demand: households and businesses need clearer long-term incentives to electrify.

turns.speaker: Manuela Perteghella
turns.text: Are the Warm Homes Plan and Boiler Upgrade Scheme enough, especially for off-grid homes?

turns.speaker: Adam Berman
turns.text: They help, and recent increases for off-grid homes are welcome, but uptake of heat pumps is still tiny and the 'spark gap'—electricity vs gas prices—must close to make electrification broadly attractive.

turns.speaker: Manuela Perteghella
turns.text: What practical steps would encourage people to install heat pumps and retrofit homes?

turns.speaker: Adam Berman
turns.text: A long-term glide path: stable subsidies that phase down predictably, more installers and accreditation, financing options, and a clear plan to lower electricity operating costs over time.

turns.speaker: Adam Berman
turns.text: Small, abrupt cuts to programmes and grants create uncertainty. We need a joined-up plan—planning, installers, finance and electricity-costs working together.

chapters.title: Competitiveness, carbon pricing and revenue recycling
chapters.takeaway: Taxes that raise costs without targeted recycling risk pushing production abroad; industries ask for level playing fields, clearer carbon-leakage protection and use of revenues to support decarbonisation.

turns.speaker: Sammy Wilson
turns.text: Do environmental taxes in your sectors actually change investment, as the Treasury claims?

turns.speaker: Andrew McDermott
turns.text: Not positively in ceramics. Energy can be up to 50% of production cost; taxes that raise costs make us uncompetitive and drive output offshore rather than fund genuine decarbonisation.

turns.speaker: Andrew McDermott
turns.text: We see imports rising while domestic output falls. Territorial emissions fall, but consumption emissions—emissions tied to what we buy—can rise. Policy monitoring misses that.

turns.speaker: Matthew Croucher
turns.text: The motor sector is improving environmental performance, but high UK electricity costs—many times EU averages—make electrifying industrial processes, like paint shops, very expensive.

turns.speaker: Adam Berman
turns.text: The electricity sector shows a balanced approach can work: carbon pricing plus targeted subsidies like Contracts for Difference drove down emissions from generation steeply.

turns.speaker: Sammy Wilson
turns.text: Should carbon-tax revenue be recycled to help industries decarbonise?

turns.speaker: Andrew McDermott
turns.text: Yes. The EU ETS has clearer revenue-recycling to support industry. In the UK we have hit-and-miss schemes; more systematic recycling is needed to preserve competitiveness.

turns.speaker: Adam Berman
turns.text: I agree that a mix of 'stick' and 'carrot' is needed. A carrot-only approach would be far costlier. But revenue use should be targeted to lower operating costs—especially electricity—for industry to invest.

turns.speaker: Manuela Perteghella
turns.text: Could fossil-fuel revenues—like those from Jackdaw—be ringfenced to fund the transition?

turns.speaker: Adam Berman
turns.text: They could and that makes sense for transition and regional just transition support, but those revenues are relatively small versus the total investment needed—private capital will fund most of it.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Final practical asks from you three?

turns.speaker: Matthew Croucher
turns.text: Give industry long-term certainty on tax and regulation, consult more on timing—especially for eVED—and tackle public-charging costs and residual-value risks for EVs.

turns.speaker: Andrew McDermott
turns.text: Make electricity cheaper for industry, broaden access to schemes like BICS, and adopt metrics that include imports and consumption emissions so policy doesn't simply offshore emissions.

turns.speaker: Adam Berman
turns.text: Set a clear long-term electrification plan, close the spark gap to favour electricity for heat, support installer capacity and finance, and use targeted revenue recycling to ease the transition.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you—your evidence on timing, costs, competitiveness and the need for clearer long-term signals will feed into our report.
